_README: Reading-comprehension items for the TwistBench human preference study, one per pool story.
Roger Beaty and John Walkiewicz asked for distractors tied to the story itself: drawing them
from other stories' reveals let anyone who read the first page eliminate them on setting and
characters alone, so the item tested 'did you open this' rather than 'did you read the ending'.
- All four options use the SAME story's characters and setting, so nothing but the ending
- The correct option is authored in the same voice and length band as the distractors. Using
the LLM `reveal` annotation for the correct one and hand-written text for the rest would
- Every distractor is verified FALSE against the story text, not against the annotation. (The
annotation for anthropic_claude-sonnet-4-5__t09__s01 is itself wrong: it says Marcus's
sister never existed, but the story's memorial wall confirms she was real and died.)
- Distractors are plausible endings for that setup, not absurd ones.
The builder fails if any pool story is missing here or has other than 3 distractors.

after-twenty-years.correct: The man waiting is a criminal wanted in Chicago; the first policeman was Jimmy Wells himself, who could not make the arrest and sent a plain-clothes officer to do it.
distractors: Jimmy Wells never came at all, and a note tells the waiting man that his friend had died years before.
Both men had turned criminal in the twenty years apart, and each had come to the meeting meaning to hand in the other.
The man waiting in the doorway was Jimmy Wells, and the friend he had been expecting was the policeman who first spoke to him.

anthropic_claude-sonnet-4-5__t10__s08.correct: Eleanor's stories were true: she had run an escape network for children during the war and been formally honoured for it, and her family had dismissed all of it as invention.
distractors: Eleanor had invented the whole wartime history, and the documents in her file turn out to have been forged by Eleanor herself.
Eleanor had not rescued anyone but had worked for the occupiers, which is why her family would never speak about the war.
Maya discovers that Eleanor was her own grandmother, given up for adoption decades before they met.

chickamauga.correct: The child is a deaf mute, who has heard nothing of the battle he has been playing among, and the dead woman at the burning house is his mother.
distractors: The child had been dreaming the whole march, and wakes unharmed in his own bed as the story closes.
The child is blind, and has been feeling his way through a forest he was never able to see.
The crawling men the child leads turn out to be his father's regiment, come to carry him home.

anthropic_claude-sonnet-4-5__t09__s01.correct: Marcus's sister was the real Dr. Sarah Morrison, who died; he had taken her name and fixated on the narrator because she shares it and had filled his sister's post.
distractors: Marcus had invented his sister entirely, and hospital records show that no Dr. Sarah Morrison had ever worked there.
Marcus was himself a psychiatrist who had lost his licence, and had posed as a volunteer in order to observe the narrator.
The narrator discovers that she had treated Marcus's sister years earlier and failed to prevent her death.

desirees-baby.correct: An old letter from his mother reveals that it is Armand, not his wife, who belongs to the race he had condemned her for.
distractors: A letter reveals that his wife's unknown parents had both been white, and that his accusation had been baseless from the start.
Armand had known his wife's origins before he married her, and had hidden them from his own family for years.
The child was not Armand's at all, and the bundle of old letters reveals an earlier attachment of hers.

anthropic_claude-sonnet-4-5__t09__s05.correct: Rachel had deliberately caused a patient's death because he was responsible for Sarah's father's, then killed her own mother to stop her exposing it.
distractors: Margaret took her own life after discovering that Rachel had been stealing drugs from her patients for years.
It was Margaret who had caused the patient's death, and Rachel had spent years covering for her mother.
Sarah's own father had been the surgeon at fault, and Rachel's crimes turn out to have nothing to do with him.

dusk.correct: The cake of soap belonged to the elderly gentleman from the bench, not to the young man, so the hard-luck story had been a lie after all.
distractors: The young man returns the sovereign the following day with interest, proving that his story had been true all along.
The elderly gentleman turns out to be the young man's father, who had sent him to test Gortsby's charity.
Gortsby discovers his own wallet gone, lifted while he was hunting through the dusk for the young man.

anthropic_claude-sonnet-4-5__t10__s04.correct: The woman calling herself Rebecca was an impostor working for the people Sarah had threatened, exposed when her description of Sarah matched nobody.
distractors: Rebecca was genuine, and it was Sarah who had faked her own death and been in hiding the whole time.
The letter had been written by Sarah before she died, as a test of whether Claire would keep looking.
Rebecca was an undercover police officer who had been quietly protecting Claire from the start.

horseman-in-the-sky.correct: The horseman that Druse shot from the cliff was his own father.
distractors: The horseman was Druse's commanding officer, who had ridden out to test whether the sentries were awake.
Druse had fired deliberately wide, and the horse had gone over the edge of its own accord.
The officer who watched the horse fall was Druse's father, and never learned who had fired the shot.

anthropic_claude-sonnet-4-5__t09__s00.correct: Charlotte's grandmother had been an intelligence agent during the Cold War, her file sealed for decades at her own request.
distractors: The papers in the attic had belonged to a previous owner of the house and had nothing to do with her grandmother.
Her grandmother had been watched for decades as a suspected foreign agent, and the suspicion had been wrong.
It was Charlotte's grandfather who had been the agent, and her grandmother had spent her life covering for him.

luck.correct: The celebrated soldier is in fact a fool, and every honour he holds records a blunder that happened to turn out well.
distractors: The soldier's victories had been real, but he had taken the credit for plans the narrator drew up for him.
The narrator had secretly coached him before every examination and every battle, and directed each move he made.
The soldier had always known he was incompetent, and had tried repeatedly to resign and been refused each time.

anthropic_claude-sonnet-4-5__t09__s08.correct: Margaret had been following her estranged daughter's life through anonymous accounts online, and died alone of natural causes with the cookies still in the oven.
distractors: Margaret had been killed by her daughter, who had come back to the apartment that night after all.
The letter was a forgery and Margaret had no daughter, having invented her over many years.
Margaret had been poisoned slowly over several months by a neighbour who wanted the apartment.

necklace.correct: The borrowed necklace had been paste, worth five hundred francs, and the ten years of poverty had been for nothing.
distractors: Her friend had known about the substitution from the beginning, and had said nothing while she paid.
The necklace had never been lost at all: it had slipped into the lining of her cloak and stayed there.
The replacement she bought was itself a fake, and the debt she spent ten years paying had been a fraud.

anthropic_claude-sonnet-4-5__t12__s03.correct: David had not left willingly: Sarah's sister and Richard staged the assault and the restraining order to keep them apart, and Sarah went on to marry Richard.
distractors: David had left of his own accord to escape gambling debts, exactly as Sarah had believed for thirty years.
Sarah's memory of the accident was false, and she had staged her own injury in order to end the relationship.
Tom, who wrote the letter, had been the one who attacked Sarah, and had blamed Richard to clear himself.

the-jewelry.correct: The jewellery he had always dismissed as paste was real and worth a fortune, and he sells it, leaves his post, and marries again badly.
distractors: The jewellery was paste after all, and the jeweller who offered him a fortune had been running a swindle.
His wife had inherited the jewels from a family she had never once spoken of to him.
His wife had been buying the jewels quietly with money taken from his employer's accounts.

anthropic_claude-sonnet-4-5__t12__s06.correct: The father had a second son he had never acknowledged, whom he had quietly kept photographs of for years.
distractors: The father's secret was a second family abroad, which the narrator's mother had known about from the beginning.
The other man was not the father's son at all, but a student he had mentored after his own children left home.
The father had been preparing to leave the family, and the letters were the proof of it.

the-last-leaf.correct: The last leaf had been painted on the wall by the old artist downstairs, who caught pneumonia doing it in the storm and died of it.
distractors: Sue had tied the last real leaf to the vine herself, to stop Johnsy giving up.
The ivy was an evergreen variety, so the last leaf was never going to fall at all.
The old artist had painted Johnsy's portrait rather than the leaf, and it was the portrait that gave her hope.

anthropic_claude-sonnet-4-5__t12__s00.correct: Margaret is not a grieving widow but the deliberate killer of her husband and his associates, using the assumptions people make about her blindness to escape suspicion.
distractors: Her husband's death really had been an accident, and her confession is a delusion brought on by grief.
Her guide dog's trainer had committed the killings, and Margaret had been shielding him throughout.
The detective had killed her husband himself, and Margaret had quietly worked out how he did it.
